doc.title: Dave Bennett interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 16, 2025

title: Versatility, 'I don't like jazz but...' and bringing joy
summary: Bennett says audiences are pleasantly surprised, the word jazz scares some away, and he wants shows to be a joyful conversation rather than education.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well I admire you for your fashioning a career that is — I’ve heard people say, I mean you and I do a lot of the same things, and sometimes I’ve heard people tell me well I don’t know what to expect when I go to one of your gigs. And as if that’s not a good thing. Have you ever had anybody like question your versatility?

Only if they’ve never heard us. You know. So there’s been times where people will say, after the show they say, I guess it’s a compliment, where they would say, “I heard this was a jazz concert.” And they say, “I don’t like jazz but I love what you guys did.” Unfortunately I think nowadays the word “jazz” scares people away a lot of times, © Fillius Jazz Archive -17-

because they have a preconceived idea of what they might be getting. Like to them maybe jazz is something really far out that they don’t understand. Where just like rock, there are several different types. So that’s an interesting thing I’ve noticed. But no, every time people after the show, they’re always surprised in a good way. And you’re just trying to lure them in you know.
One word that I don’t think is connected to jazz now enough is joy.
Like jazz is heavy and it’s up here. And the fact that you spread joy, I think you just described it, when people say, “I don’t like jazz but I liked what you did.”

Yeah I don’t quite understand the — like that seriousness, you know, that darkness. Again everybody has their own approach to it. And if they want to be more serious about it that’s their thing. But for me if you’re up there performing for people, I think it should be more of a conversation. I remember hearing somebody say, “Well you know it’s our job to educate the audience.” And I was like, “Oh come on, lighten up, lighten up.” For one thing that sounds really pompous. And second of all no, we’re there to give them a break, to give them something to enjoy. And my own approach to things is when you’re on stage, no matter where you are, make it more of a conversation. You know we’re all in the same spot here you know and I think if you just approach it that way people can feel it. Because an audience can feel if you’re distant or not, and I think they want to be able to connect with you. Why not? First of all it’s a miracle that any of us can do this for a living. Right? And it’s getting harder. It’s getting harder. I mean there’s not as many places to play as there was 30 years ago, so the fact that we’re out there able to do this, let’s squeeze every ounce of enjoyment and joy that we can out of this you know. At least that’s the way I think about it.
